The top 10 courses in demand in UK for 2027 include healthcare, medicine, computer science, artificial intelligence, data science, cybersecurity, engineering, construction, finance, business analytics and life sciences.

These fields stand out because they connect with occupations where the UK is seeing strong hiring demand, projected workforce growth or persistent skills needs.

That does not mean choosing one of these courses guarantees a job. Far from it. A degree works best when the subject matches your ability, the course teaches practical skills and you graduate with some evidence that you can use those skills.

For students comparing options for 2027, the more useful question is simple: which course gives you a realistic route from university into work?

How We Chose the Most In-Demand Courses for 2027

This is not a list of subjects that happen to be popular with international students.

We looked at current occupational demand, projected employment growth, the connection between courses and priority occupations, and the range of careers each subject can support.

The UK's 2026 Skills England annual report identifies 150 priority occupations across major sectors. Employment in those occupations is projected to rise from about 7.6 million in 2025 to 9.5 million by 2035, an increase of roughly 1.8 million jobs. Digital, engineering and construction occupations appear particularly frequently across the priority sectors.

Current demand tells a similar story. The Department for Education's Occupations in Demand 2025 analysis identifies 62 occupations in critical demand, accounting for about 5.1 million workers. Specialist medical practitioners recorded the strongest overall demand in the analysis, while IT business analysts, architects and systems designers were also in the critical-demand category.

That gives us a better foundation than simply calling a subject "future-proof".

1. Nursing and Allied Health

Healthcare is one of the clearest answers to which courses are in demand in UK because it connects students to occupations the country continually needs.

Nursing is the obvious example, but the opportunity is broader. Students can study adult nursing, mental health nursing, children's nursing, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, radiography and other allied health subjects.

The Department for Education reports that health and social care has the largest number of workers employed in high-demand occupations.

For nurses, the National Careers Service career profile currently gives an indicative salary range of £32,000 to £48,000.

Popular options include:

  • Adult Nursing
  • Mental Health Nursing
  • Children's Nursing
  • Physiotherapy
  • Occupational Therapy
  • Diagnostic Radiography

One practical detail matters here. Professional recognition can be more important than a university's headline ranking. If you want to become a registered professional, make sure the course actually supports the required registration route.

International applicants can also check how nursing study routes work for overseas students before choosing universities.

2. Medicine

Medicine is demanding to enter, expensive to study and takes years of training.

It is still one of the most in-demand degrees in the UK.

The government's occupational analysis places specialist medical practitioners at the top of its current demand measures.

A UK medical degree normally takes about five years, followed by foundation and specialist training. The National Careers Service profile for hospital doctors gives an indicative earnings range of £40,000 to £145,000, depending heavily on experience and stage of training.

Medicine suits students who are academically strong, comfortable with a long training route and genuinely interested in clinical work. Choosing it simply because doctors can earn well is a poor reason to spend five or more years studying it.

Applicants considering this path should understand what international students need to study medicine in the UK before building a shortlist.

3. Computer Science and Software Engineering

Almost every large industry now relies on software.

Banks need it. Hospitals need it. Retailers, manufacturers, universities and public services do too.

That makes computer science one of the strongest high-demand courses in UK for students who want transferable technical skills.

Skills England identifies programmers and software development professionals as a priority across seven sectors, more than any other occupation in its cross-sector analysis. It also projects around 192,000 additional programmers and software development professionals between 2025 and 2035, although projections around AI-exposed digital occupations carry extra uncertainty.

Relevant courses include:

  • Computer Science
  • Software Engineering
  • Information Technology
  • Cloud Computing
  • Computer Science with AI
  • Financial Technology

Software developers currently have an indicative salary range of £30,000 to £75,000 on the National Careers Service.

There is a mildly counterintuitive point here. Learning more programming languages does not automatically make a student more employable. Strong problem solving, software engineering fundamentals, projects and work experience can matter more than knowing the syntax of ten languages.

Students comparing this field can look at universities with established computing departments.

4. Artificial Intelligence and Data Science

AI gets plenty of attention, but businesses cannot do much with AI if their data is poor.

That is why data science, machine learning, statistics and AI increasingly overlap.

A supermarket provides a simple example. It may collect millions of transactions but still struggle to understand why a product sells well in Manchester and poorly in Bristol. Analysts can combine sales, stock, pricing and customer data to identify what is actually happening.

Popular study routes include:

  • Artificial Intelligence
  • Data Science
  • Machine Learning
  • Statistics and Data Analytics
  • Computer Science with AI
  • Business Analytics

The National Careers Service data scientist profile currently shows an indicative salary range of £32,000 to £83,000.

For students asking which course is best for future careers, AI and data science deserve serious consideration. But course content matters more than branding. A programme with solid statistics, programming, databases and applied projects may be more valuable than one that simply puts "AI" in its title.

If your interest is specifically technical, you can compare the wider range of IT study routes available in the UK.

5. Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity remains important, but the employment picture deserves a realistic explanation.

The UK government's latest cyber labour-market research estimates a cyber workforce of roughly 143,000 people and an annual workforce gap of about 3,800 professionals. It also found that 49% of UK businesses had a basic technical cyber skills gap and 30% had gaps in more advanced technical areas.

At the same time, advertised cyber vacancies fell during 2024. Entry-level demand has become more competitive.

That makes practical experience especially important.

Useful courses include:

  • Cybersecurity
  • Network Security
  • Digital Forensics
  • Ethical Hacking
  • Cloud Security
  • Computer Science with Cybersecurity

The same government research recorded a £55,000 median advertised salary for core cyber roles in 2024, but almost two-thirds of those job adverts asked for two to six years of experience.

That is a useful reality check. Cybersecurity can be a strong career, but graduates should not assume a degree alone will take them directly into a £55,000 job.

Labs, placements, certifications and genuine technical projects make a difference.

6. Engineering and Clean Energy

Engineering sits behind many of the projects governments and businesses want to build over the next decade.

Transport systems, power networks, buildings, manufacturing, renewable energy and defence all need engineers.

Skills England identifies engineering professions across several priority sectors and expects the clean-energy priority workforce to grow particularly quickly. Its current projections suggest a rise of more than 70% in priority clean-energy occupations between 2025 and 2035, though the report warns that sector projections should be treated as broad indicators rather than precise forecasts.

Relevant degrees include:

  • Civil Engineering
  • Mechanical Engineering
  • Electrical Engineering
  • Electronic Engineering
  • Renewable Energy Engineering
  • Energy Systems Engineering

For one representative career, civil engineers have an indicative salary range of £29,000 to £63,000 according to the National Careers Service.

Students who enjoy mathematics, physics and solving tangible problems may find engineering offers something valuable: the skills connect to projects people can actually see being built.

7. Architecture, Construction and the Built Environment

Technology receives much of the attention in discussions about future careers. Construction is easier to overlook.

It should not be.

Skills England projects roughly 493,000 additional workers in priority construction occupations by 2035. Construction is one of the sectors expected to require some of the largest increases in workforce numbers.

Relevant study options include:

  • Architecture
  • Construction Management
  • Quantity Surveying
  • Building Surveying
  • Civil Engineering
  • Building Services Engineering

Architecture also has a relatively direct connection between specialist higher education and priority occupations.

The National Careers Service currently lists an indicative architect salary range of £31,000 to £58,000.

For students who enjoy both analytical and creative work, the built environment can offer a useful middle ground between design, technology and practical delivery.

8. Accounting, Finance and FinTech

AI can automate calculations. It cannot remove the need for financial judgement.

Organisations still need people who can interpret accounts, assess risk, understand regulation, manage budgets and explain what financial information actually means.

Skills England identifies financial managers and directors as priority occupations across four of the sectors in its analysis.

Useful degrees include:

  • Accounting and Finance
  • Finance
  • Financial Technology
  • Economics and Finance
  • Banking and Investment
  • Risk Management

A management accountant can earn an indicative £30,000 to £60,000, according to the National Careers Service.

Professional exemptions can also matter. A degree that gives useful exemptions towards recognised accounting qualifications may offer more practical value than a slightly higher university ranking.

That detail is easy to miss when students compare courses only by league tables.

9. Business Analytics and Digital Business

Business remains popular, but general business study is not automatically the strongest route into employment.

Adding analytical or technical skills can change the picture.

Business analytics teaches students how to use data to understand customers, operations, pricing, supply chains and performance. It can lead towards roles that sit between technical teams and management.

Relevant programmes include:

  • Business Analytics
  • Digital Business
  • Business Information Systems
  • Supply Chain Analytics
  • Digital Marketing
  • Project Management

The National Careers Service business analyst profile gives an indicative salary range of £23,000 to £55,000 and notes that internships or business experience during a degree can provide an advantage.

Skills England also offers a useful warning. Business and management courses produce many graduates who enter priority occupations, but the proportion is lower than for more specialised subjects such as computing, engineering, health and architecture.

So if you choose business, specialise where it makes sense.

Students interested in this direction can compare universities with strong business-focused programmes.

10. Pharmacy and Life Sciences

Life sciences sit at the intersection of healthcare, research, technology and industry.

Skills England projects the priority workforce in life sciences to grow by around 44% between 2025 and 2035. Again, these are broad workforce projections rather than guarantees for individual graduates.

Relevant degrees include:

  • Pharmacy
  • Biomedical Science
  • Biotechnology
  • Biochemistry
  • Pharmacology
  • Pharmaceutical Science

These courses do not all lead to the same type of career.

Pharmacy follows a regulated professional route. Biomedical science, biotechnology and pharmacology may lead towards laboratories, diagnostics, research, pharmaceutical companies or further study.

For pharmacists, the National Careers Service gives an indicative salary range of £40,000 to £65,000. It also confirms that becoming a pharmacist requires an approved MPharm degree followed by foundation training.

The short answer is this: decide on the likely career first, then choose the life-science degree that actually leads towards it.

Which Courses Have the Best Job Opportunities in the UK?

For students focused mainly on employment, healthcare, computer science, engineering, data-related subjects and some regulated professional degrees currently show particularly strong links with areas of labour-market demand.

There is no single course that wins every comparison.

A nursing degree leads towards a clearly defined profession. Computer science can open doors across many industries. Engineering can take graduates into infrastructure, energy, manufacturing or consultancy.

Those are very different advantages.

If you are still deciding between broad subject areas rather than specifically looking for labour-market demand, it makes more sense to compare UK degree choices from a wider academic perspective.

Which Course Is Best for the Future in the UK?

For 2027 entrants, some of the strongest future-facing areas include software, AI and data, healthcare, engineering, clean energy and life sciences.

Skills England expects programmers and software developers, IT business analysts and several engineering occupations to contribute significantly to future priority employment growth.

But there is a catch.

The course best for the future is not necessarily the course with the newest name.

A solid computer science programme covering software engineering, algorithms, databases and mathematics may age better than a narrowly designed degree based around one current AI platform.

Tools change quickly. Strong underlying skills last longer.

Which In-Demand Courses Can Lead to Higher Salaries?

Medicine, data science, software development, finance, pharmacy and some engineering careers can lead to relatively high earnings.

That does not make salary comparison straightforward.

The £32,000 to £83,000 range currently shown for data scientists, for example, covers starter through experienced workers. It should not be read as a promise that a new graduate will earn £83,000.

The same applies across this article.

Look at salary as one part of the decision, alongside employability, training length, tuition fees, professional registration and the kind of work you actually want to do.

How Much Do In-Demand Courses Cost in the UK?

There is no single tuition fee for an in-demand course.

University, degree level and subject all matter.

The British Council's current guide to UK study costs puts international undergraduate tuition at roughly £11,400 to £38,000 per year and international postgraduate tuition at approximately £9,000 to £30,000. Medicine and some specialist laboratory-based programmes can cost more, so applicants should always check the current course page before budgeting.

Living costs need to be added separately. The same British Council guidance suggests roughly £1,300 to £1,400 per month in London and around £900 to £1,300 per month elsewhere in the UK for a student without dependants.

If cost is becoming the deciding factor, you can compare lower-cost university options outside the most expensive choices.

Can Scholarships Reduce the Cost?

Yes, but eligibility varies.

One concrete example is the GREAT Scholarships programme. For the 2026-27 academic year, eligible Bangladeshi postgraduate applicants can receive £10,000 towards tuition fees at participating UK universities for selected one-year taught postgraduate courses.

What International Students Should Know for 2027

Students planning to use post-study time to build UK work experience need to know about a significant change.

That makes career preparation during the degree more important.

When comparing universities, look beyond modules and rankings. Check whether the course offers:

  • a placement or internship;
  • employer projects;
  • professional accreditation where relevant;
  • practical laboratory or technical work;
  • careers support; and
  • opportunities to build experience before graduation.

For students targeting an early-year start, it is also worth checking which UK universities offer January entry.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the top 10 courses in demand in UK for 2027?

The top 10 courses in demand in UK for 2027 include nursing and allied health, medicine, computer science and software engineering, AI and data science, cybersecurity, engineering and clean energy, architecture and construction, accounting and finance, business analytics, and pharmacy or life sciences.

These subjects align with several areas of current or projected UK employment demand.

Which courses are most in demand in the UK?

Healthcare, medical, digital, software, engineering and some construction-related occupations feature strongly in current government demand data. The best course still depends on the student's academic background and intended career.

Which course is best for job in UK?

There is no degree that guarantees employment. Nursing and other regulated healthcare courses offer relatively direct professional routes, while computing, engineering and data-related degrees can provide skills used by employers across several industries.

Which course is best for future?

Computer science, AI and data, healthcare, engineering, clean energy and life sciences all have strong future demand signals. Students should still prioritise durable skills, work experience and a course with clear career outcomes.

Which IT courses are in demand in UK?

Computer science, software engineering, artificial intelligence, data science, cybersecurity and related digital courses connect with several important skill areas. For a technology-only comparison, explore the different UK IT degree routes and specialisations.

Which courses in the UK can lead to high-paying careers?

Medicine, data science, software development, finance, engineering and pharmacy can lead to strong earnings at experienced levels. Starting salaries are usually lower, and pay depends on the actual occupation rather than the degree title alone.

Final Thoughts

The top 10 courses in demand in UK are not simply the subjects attracting the most applications.

The stronger choices connect education with real work.

Healthcare needs skilled professionals. Digital industries need software, data and security expertise. Infrastructure and clean energy need engineers. Finance and business need analytical judgement.

Still, demand should not make the decision for you.

A student who dislikes coding is unlikely to build a great career in software simply because software developers are needed. The same applies to medicine, engineering or finance.

Look for the overlap between three things: skills the UK needs, skills employers value and a subject you can become genuinely good at.

That is a much better way to choose a course for 2027.

Once you have narrowed the subject, you can plan the wider UK study process, including course selection, applications and the next steps towards university.
